bonds_big.h:
THE BIG PICTURE · AS OF OCT 30
Treasuries rallied again on Friday as a tech-earnings rout sent the Nasdaq down about 3%: the 10-year was near 4.93% in the afternoon, about 5 bp below Thursday's 4.98% close, after touching about 4.89%, its lowest since Sept 10. That caps an October drop of about 36 bp, the biggest monthly rally since 2024. December hike odds slipped to about 72% from 79% a day earlier.
~4.93% 10-yr, Fri afternoon−7 bp since last Friday−36 bp in October
📍 What's happening
  • A flight to safety. Intel fell about 30% on a weak forecast and Amazon disappointed, a day after Alphabet's 12% drop; the Nasdaq was down about 3.1% and the S&P 500 2.1% Friday afternoon, and money moved into Treasuries.
  • Hike odds eased. December hike odds fell to about 72% on Kalshi and Polymarket from 79% on Thursday, and a January hike to about 26% from 33%. The Fed held at 3.75–4.00% on Oct 28 with two dissents for a hike.
  • Wage growth is cooling. The Q3 employment cost index rose 0.8%, as expected, and private wages rose 3.1% from a year earlier, the slowest since 2021, even with September core PCE at 3.1%.
  • Credit lagged the rally. The high-yield spread widened 12 bp to 326 bp on Oct 29 and the IG spread to 89 bp, though both stay below Oct 23 levels; Microsoft's $25B bond sale still drew $115B of orders.
🏢 What it means for real estate
  • Fixed-rate debt is cheaper than a month ago. The 10-year is about 38 bp below its Oct 5 high of 5.31%, while a likely December hike would still lift SOFR-based floating loans.
  • Mortgage rates should keep easing. Freddie Mac's 30-year was 7.24% on Oct 29, the lowest this month but 107 bp above a year ago; Friday's lower yields are not yet in that survey.
  • Distress is trading. Boston office sales reached $2.2B in Q3 (Avison Young), including 100 Summer St. at about $236/SF, 68% below 2019; the Hyatt Centric Faneuil Hall sold for $58.4M with $40M of bank debt.
  • Leverage is still thin. Multifamily and industrial cap rates (~5.20%) sit about 27 bp over the 10-year, versus 230–340 bp historically, and multifamily CMBS delinquency is 8.04%.
🧭 Where we think it's headed
Most likely4.75–5.05%

Yields hold most of October's rally through year-end. A December hike stays the base case, but slower wage growth and wobbly tech stocks keep buyers in Treasuries while Brent holds near $105–$115.

Growth scare or truce4.45–4.75%

The tech selloff spreads, a weak Nov 6 jobs report pulls December hike odds below even, or U.S.–Iran talks push oil down.

Hawkish turn5.05–5.35%

A strong jobs report, a hot October CPI on Nov 10, new attacks on Gulf shipping or bigger auction sizes at the Nov 4 refunding push yields back toward the 5.31% high of Oct 5.

▲ Risks that push yields higher
  1. A December hike. Still about 72% priced (Oct 30); two officials already voted for a hike on Oct 28.
  2. Oil and the Gulf. Brent rose about 1.5% to near $112.50 on Oct 30 after tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz; U.S. diesel is $6.352, up $2.634 from a year ago.
  3. Sticky inflation. PCE is 3.6% and core 3.1%; CPI was 3.7% and PPI 6.3% from a year earlier in September.
  4. Strong growth. Q3 GDP grew 3.4% and final sales to private domestic purchasers 4.9%, which argues against any easing.
  5. Refunding supply. Borrowing estimates on Nov 2 and the Nov 4 refunding set the 3-, 10- and 30-year sizes for Nov 9–12; a bigger borrowing need would mean more supply.
  6. Corporate supply. Microsoft's $25B sale adds to more than $500B of AI-related debt this year, competing with Treasuries for buyers.
▼ Things that could pull yields lower
  1. A deeper AI unwind. Intel, Amazon and Alphabet results have raised doubts about debt-funded AI spending; two days of tech losses drove this week's rally.
  2. Cooling wages. Private wage growth slowed to 3.1%, the least since 2021, and real wages fell 0.6% over the year.
  3. Softer jobs. September payrolls rose just 29,000; a weak Nov 6 report could pull December hike odds further down.
  4. A deal with Iran. A reported U.S. letter to Iran aimed at reviving talks; lower oil would ease inflation fears.

bonds_head.h: Who is borrowing, how much, and at what price: Treasury auctions, jumbo corporate and municipal deals, and credit spreads. Treasuries rallied again on Friday as a tech-earnings rout sent the Nasdaq down about 3%: the 10-year was near 4.93% in the afternoon, capping an October drop of about 36 bp. Credit moved the other way on Thursday, when the high-yield spread widened 12 bp to 326 bp and the investment-grade spread to 89 bp. Microsoft's $25B bond sale, its first since 2017, drew $115B of orders, and this week's $211B of 2-, 5- and 7-year notes and FRNs sold without trouble.

bonds_tsy.h: This week's $211B of 2-, 5- and 7-year notes and FRNs is done, and demand improved after a soft start. The $70B 5-year sold at 4.845% with a 0.4 bp tail and a 2.33x bid-to-cover, up from 2.21x in September; the $28B 2-year FRN drew 3.05x; and Thursday's $44B 7-year cleared at 4.894% with no tail and a 2.46x bid-to-cover vs. a 2.49x average, leaving dealers 9.4%. Monday's $69B 2-year had tailed 0.3 bp. There are no coupon auctions next week; the November refunding follows with 3-year notes Mon, Nov 9, 10-year notes Tue, Nov 10 and 30-year bonds Thu, Nov 12, with sizes set Nov 4 (August guidance points to $58B, $42B and $25B).

bonds_tsy_note.h: Treasury posts borrowing estimates at 3:00 PM ET on Nov 2 and its quarterly refunding on Nov 4, which sets the November 3-, 10- and 30-year sizes and says whether coupon sizes stay flat for at least the next several quarters; a buyback of at least $4B of 10- to 20-year bonds runs the same day. The 10-year sale on Nov 10 comes the same morning as October CPI.

cap_caps.h: Core cap rates by sector against a 10-year of about 4.93% on Friday afternoon (4.98% at Thursday's close). Multifamily and industrial, both at 5.20%, price about 27 bp above the 10-year, versus 2010–2020 average spreads of 230 bp and 340 bp; strip retail at 6.40% and office at 7.40% sit about 147 bp and 247 bp above, against historical averages of 320 bp and 280 bp, and hotel at 8.50% is about 357 bp above, with no historical average given. Recent Boston trades show the gap between sectors: the Hyatt Centric Faneuil Hall sold for $58.4M (about $358K per room) on Oct 29, while 100 Summer St. went at a foreclosure auction for about $236/SF, 68% below its 2019 price.

cap_cmbs.h: CMBS delinquency by property type in September (Trepp). Office is still the stress point at 12.16%, up from 12.00% in August, and multifamily rose to 8.04% from 7.69%, passing retail, which fell to 6.58% from 7.20%. Lodging rose to 6.18% and industrial held at 1.14%. October figures are due in early November. Trepp counts $78B of CMBS loans reaching hard maturity from October 2026 through 2027, and Boston office losses are showing up in sales: 100 Summer St. sold for $260M against $470M of 2019 financing, and 18 Tremont St. for $30M against a $103M 2019 price.

cap_cost.h: Building costs keep climbing: the Turner Building Cost Index rose 1.48% in Q3 to 1,575, up 5.49% from a year earlier, and construction input prices were up 11.7% year over year in September, led by diesel (+115.2%), energy (+69.9%) and metals. Construction hourly earnings are up 4.3% and employment 1.3% over the year, while economy-wide private wage growth slowed to 3.1% in Q3, the slowest since 2021. U.S. diesel rose to $6.352 in the latest week and Brent was back near $112.50 on Oct 30; October PPI on Nov 13 will show whether input inflation is cooling, so replacement costs remain high.

cap_fed.h: Prediction markets still favor a December hike, but less than a day ago: about 72% on Oct 30 (Kalshi 71.5%, Polymarket 72.5%, 11:26 AM ET), down from 79% on Kalshi on Oct 29 after an in-line employment cost report and a tech-stock selloff. CME FedWatch was also near 72%. The Fed held at 3.75–4.00% on Oct 28 with two dissents for a hike. Kalshi puts a January 2027 hike at about 26%, down from 33%.

cap_fed_note.h: December and January odds are a snapshot from Oct 30, 11:26 AM ET; the March 2027 hike figure (about 54%) is from Oct 29. December hike odds are 72%, down from 79% on Oct 29, and January hike odds fell to 26% from 33%. Each meeting is priced as its own market. Next: Treasury borrowing estimates at 3:00 PM on Nov 2, Election Day and JOLTS at 10:00 AM on Nov 3, the quarterly refunding on Nov 4 and the October jobs report at 8:30 AM on Nov 6.

cap_fuel.h: Diesel moved up again while gasoline eased: for the week of Oct 26, U.S. diesel is $6.352 a gallon (up 7.6¢ on the week and $2.634 from a year ago) and regular gasoline $4.269 (down 1.5¢, up $1.234 from a year ago). New England diesel slipped to $6.421 and gasoline to $4.199, with Boston gasoline at $4.176. Brent rose about 1.5% to near $112.50 on Oct 30 after tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, reversing part of Thursday's drop to $110.80. The next EIA prices come Nov 2. Diesel feeds construction, trucking and heating costs (diesel producer prices were up 115.2% year over year in September), and gasoline squeezes what renters and retail tenants have left to spend.

cap_opex.h: Property insurance is getting cheaper: commercial property premiums fell 6.3% in Q2, the fourth straight quarterly decline, though umbrella liability rose 5.3%. Energy is going the other way: winter heating oil costs are projected up 31% per household, Eversource NH's winter rate is 17.32¢ per kWh (up 10%), and New England diesel at $6.421 a gallon keeps pressure on owner-paid heating. Labor-related costs are mixed: employer health insurance costs rose 6.4% over the year in Q3, even as private wage growth slowed to 3.1%.

cap_rates.h: Treasury curve over the past year. The 10-year was about 4.93% Friday afternoon, Oct 30, roughly 5 bp below Thursday's 4.98% close and 7 bp below last Friday's 5.00%, as a tech-stock selloff sent money into Treasuries; it touched about 4.89%, the lowest since Sept 10. It is down about 36 bp in October from 5.29% on Sept 30, about 38 bp below its 52-week high of 5.31% on Oct 5, and still up about 75 bp this year. The 2-year was near 4.58% and the 30-year 5.31%; the Fed held at 3.75–4.00% on Oct 28, and a December hike is about 72% priced.

cap_supply.h: Pipelines are shrinking in most Sun Belt metros, with 2026 deliveries projected down 47% in Austin, 40% in Phoenix and more than half in Denver, while Nashville completions are down 41%. Miami's pipeline is still expanding (above 8% of inventory) and Charlotte's is among the highest in the U.S. (above 8%). Boston has 14,523 units in its pipeline, with absorption running ahead of deliveries this year and vacancy at 5.6%; on the South Shore, the former South Weymouth air base plans up to 2,700 homes in its first phase, with two apartment complexes set to start in March 2027.

mig_fc.h: Nationally, 227,548 foreclosure filings were recorded in H1 2026, 0.16% of housing units and up 21.26% from a year earlier. Bank repossessions (REO) reached 27,983, up 33%, and foreclosure starts were 164,566, up 18%. The latest monthly figure, for August, was 40,277 filings, up 1% from the prior month and 13% from a year earlier. Florida (0.27%), South Carolina (0.26%), Delaware and Indiana (0.25%) and Illinois (0.23%) had the highest state rates in H1. Massachusetts had 2,719 filings, a rate of 0.09% (one in 1,115 units), up 3.23% from a year earlier; New Hampshire had 488, a rate of 0.08% (one in 1,329 units), up 23.54%. Both rates are well below the national rate. ATTOM's September and Q3 foreclosure reports had not been posted as of Oct 30.
